A square tile and a round coaster are each turned about their own centres through 50 degrees. Which statement about how they look afterwards is correct?
questions.a: Only the coaster looks exactly as before
o: Only the coaster looks exactly as before
Only the tile looks exactly as before

questions.a: P and Q

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about a circle.
Statement 1: A chord that passes through the centre is a diameter.
Statement 2: Every chord of a circle is a line of reflection symmetry of the circle.
Statement 3: In a circle of radius 5 units the longest chord is 10 units long.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A circle has complete rotational symmetry about its centre.
Reason (R): Every diameter of a circle is a line of reflection symmetry.
questions.a: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A circular table-top has diameter 18.6 cm in a toy model. No string pulled tight across it with ends on its edge can be longer than ___ cm.

Match each situation in Column I with the result in Column II.
Column I: 1. Locus of points 6 cm from a fixed point; 2. Locus of points equidistant from two fixed points; 3. Longest chord of a circle of radius 4 cm; 4. Lines of reflection symmetry of a regular pentagon.
Column II: a. A circle of radius 6 cm; b. 8 cm; c. The perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two points; d. 5.
True or False: If a regular hexagon and a circle with the same centre are each rotated through 37 degrees about that centre, the circle looks unchanged but the hexagon does not. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. A circle has complete rotational symmetry, so any angle leaves it unchanged. A regular hexagon looks the same only after turns that are multiples of 60 degrees, and 37 is not one.
s: States True
Reason: the circle is unchanged by any angle, the hexagon only by multiples of 60 degrees

questions.q:
A thread is pulled tight across a cart wheel with both ends on the rim and passing through the hub's centre; it measures 36 cm.
(a) What is the thread called? (b) A second thread of 40 cm is claimed to fit across the same wheel with its ends on the rim. Is that possible? Use (a).
questions.a: (a) It is a diameter, so the radius is 18 cm. (b) No. The diameter 36 cm is the longest chord, so no chord of this wheel can be 40 cm.
s: (a) Names it a diameter (a chord through the centre)
(b) Uses the diameter as the longest chord to rule out 40 cm

questions.q:
A goat is tied to a peg P by a 6 m rope and another peg Q is 8 m from P.
(a) Describe the set of points the goat can just reach with the rope fully stretched. (b) Can the goat reach Q? Give the reason using (a).
questions.a: (a) A circle with centre P and radius 6 m. (b) No, because Q is 8 m from P, which is more than the 6 m radius, so Q lies outside that circle.
s: (a) Circle with centre P and radius 6 m
(b) 8 m exceeds the radius, so Q is outside the circle

questions.q: (a) How many lines of reflection symmetry does a regular hexagon have? (b) Use (a) to find the smallest turn about its centre that leaves the hexagon looking the same, and state how a circle differs.
questions.a: (a) 6 lines. (b) 360 / 6 = 60 degrees. A circle looks the same after a turn through any angle.
s: (a) 6 lines of reflection symmetry
(b) 60 degrees, while a circle allows any angle

questions.q: Hari says the set of points equidistant from two points A and B is just the midpoint of AB. Is he right? Take A and B 10 cm apart and test a point 12 cm from the midpoint along the perpendicular to AB.
questions.a: He is wrong. The midpoint is one such point, but the whole perpendicular bisector of AB is the locus. A point 12 cm from the midpoint on it is sqrt(144 + 25) = 13 cm from both A and B.
s: States he is wrong; the locus is the whole perpendicular bisector
Tests the point: it is 13 cm from each of A and B

questions.q: Pran claims: 'In a circle of radius 5 units the longest chord is 10 units and the shortest chord is 1 unit.' Is he right? Decide whether the claim is right, wrong or partly right and justify.
questions.a: Partly right. The longest chord is the diameter, 2 x 5 = 10 units, so that half is right. There is no smallest chord: a chord pushed towards the boundary keeps shrinking and ends as a single point of length 0, so chords shorter than 1 unit exist, for example 0.5 unit.
s: Verdict: partly right
Longest chord is the diameter, 10 units
No smallest chord: chords shrink towards the edge, so lengths below 1 unit occur

questions.q: Show that no chord of a circle of radius r can be longer than 2r.
questions.a: Let AB be a chord and O the centre. OA = OB = r. If O is on AB, then AB = 2r. Otherwise OAB is a triangle and AB < OA + OB = 2r. So AB is never more than 2r.
s: Takes OA = OB = r for a chord AB
Case O on AB gives AB = 2r
Otherwise the triangle inequality gives AB < 2r

questions.q: Two lamp posts A and B stand 20 m apart. A bench is to be placed exactly as far from A as from B, and 26 m from A. Find how far from the midpoint of AB the bench can be, and how many positions are possible.
questions.a: The bench lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB. Its distance from the midpoint is sqrt(26^2 - 10^2) = sqrt(576) = 24 m. There are two positions, one on each side of AB.
s: Uses the perpendicular bisector as the locus
Distance sqrt(676 - 100) = 24 m
Two positions, one on each side

questions.q: Justify why the perpendicular bisector of AB is the locus of points equidistant from A and B, and then use it to say where the centre of a circle must lie if AB is a chord of it.
questions.a: Let M be the midpoint of AB and P any point on the perpendicular bisector. In triangles PMA and PMB, AM = BM, PM is common and the angles at M are both 90 degrees, so by SAS PA = PB: every point on the bisector is equidistant. Conversely any point equidistant from A and B lies on the bisector. Both directions hold, so the bisector is the locus. The centre O of a circle with chord AB has OA = OB (radii), so it lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
s: Every point on the bisector is equidistant, by SAS on PMA and PMB
Every equidistant point lies on the bisector
Both directions together make the bisector the locus
Applies it: OA = OB, so the centre lies on the bisector of the chord

questions.q:
A cart-maker is comparing three wheel shapes, each turning about its centre: a square, a regular hexagon and a circle.
(a) For the square and the hexagon, give the smallest turn that leaves the shape looking the same and the number of lines of reflection symmetry. (b) State what is true of the circle. (c) A point of the rim touches the ground, then again touches the ground a moment later. Explain why this makes the circle the only shape for which the wheel looks the same at all times.
questions.a: (a) Square: 90 degrees and 4 lines. Hexagon: 60 degrees and 6 lines. (b) The circle looks the same after a turn through any angle and has every diameter as a line of reflection symmetry. (c) For the circle every turn leaves it unchanged, so you cannot tell which point of the rim is touching the ground; the square and hexagon look the same only at multiples of 90 or 60 degrees, so between those they look different.
s: Square: 90 degrees and 4 lines; hexagon: 60 degrees and 6 lines
Circle: same after any turn, every diameter is a line of symmetry
Links to the wheel: any turn gives the same look, so the touching point cannot be told apart
Contrasts with the square and hexagon, which match only at multiples of 90 or 60 degrees

questions.q:
Two borewells A and B in a village are 30 m apart. The panchayat will build a water tank exactly as far from A as from B, and 25 m from each. Pipes cost Rs 300 per metre. Site 1 is on the village side of AB and needs an extra 90 m of main pipe at Rs 250 per metre. Site 2 is on the school side, needs an extra 30 m of main pipe at Rs 250 per metre and a pump costing Rs 14,000.
(a) Which line must contain every possible site? (b) How far is each site from the midpoint of AB, and how far apart are the two sites? (c) Find the total cost at each site, pipes from A and B plus the extras. (d) Recommend a site, using your totals, and state one non-cost reason that could change the choice.
questions.a: (a) The perpendicular bisector of AB. (b) sqrt(25^2 - 15^2) = 20 m from the midpoint, so the two sites are 40 m apart. (c) Pipes from A and B: 2 x 25 x 300 = Rs 15,000. Site 1: 15,000 + 90 x 250 = Rs 37,500. Site 2: 15,000 + 30 x 250 + 14,000 = Rs 36,500. (d) Site 2 is cheaper by Rs 1,000, but the saving is small, so a reason such as access to the village side or the low ground at Site 2 could favour Site 1; either choice with the figures and a reason is acceptable.
s: (a) Perpendicular bisector of AB
(b) 20 m from the midpoint; sites 40 m apart
(c) Rs 37,500 for Site 1 and Rs 36,500 for Site 2
(d) Reasoned choice using the Rs 1,000 difference and a non-cost reason

questions.q:
A school spinner toy carries the logo of a regular hexagon drawn so that its six corners lie on a circle, and the logo turns about the common centre. The designers are choosing between this logo and a plain circle.
(a) What is the smallest turn, in degrees, after which the hexagon logo looks exactly the same? (b) How many lines of reflection symmetry does the hexagon logo have, and how does that compare with the plain circle? (c) After the toy has turned through 150 degrees, will the hexagon logo look the same as at the start? How many different turns between 0 and 360 degrees (not counting 0) leave it looking the same? (d) The school wants children to see the spin. Which design should be used? Justify with your answers.
questions.a: (a) 360 / 6 = 60 degrees. (b) 6 lines, whereas the plain circle has infinitely many (every diameter). (c) 150 is not a multiple of 60, so it will look different; the turns 60, 120, 180, 240 and 300 degrees, that is 5 turns, leave it unchanged. (d) The hexagon logo, because it looks different at most turns and repeats only every 60 degrees, so the spin is visible; the plain circle looks identical after every turn, so the spin cannot be seen.
s: (a) 60 degrees
(b) 6 lines against infinitely many for the circle
(c) Different at 150 degrees; 5 turns leave it unchanged
(d) Chooses the hexagon logo, justified by repeated looks only every 60 degrees against the circle looking the same at every turn

questions.q: Two nails A and B are fixed 16 cm apart on a board. A thin circular wire ring is fitted to pass over both nails, and its centre lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB at 6 cm from the midpoint of AB. What is the radius of the ring?
questions.a: 10 cm

questions.q: A triangular plot has sides 7 m, 24 m and 25 m, and a well is to be dug at the point equally far from its three corners. Where is that point and how far is it from each corner?
questions.a: At the midpoint of the 25 m side, 12.5 m from each corner
o: At the midpoint of the 25 m side, 12.5 m from each corner
Inside the plot, 12.5 m from each corner
At the midpoint of the 25 m side, 25 m from each corner
Outside the plot, 12.5 m from each corner

questions.q: A triangular signboard has angles 35, 35 and 110 degrees, and a thin metal ring must pass through all three corners. Where is the centre of the ring in relation to the signboard?
questions.a: Outside the signboard
o: At the midpoint of its longest side
At the corner with the 110 degree angle

questions.q: Three lamp posts A, B and C stand in a straight row along a road. A contractor says one circular path can be laid through all three. Which fact shows he is wrong?
questions.a: The perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC are parallel, so no point is equally far from all three
o: The perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC are parallel, so no point is equally far from all three
The three perpendicular bisectors meet at a point on the road itself
Any three points lie on two circles, one on each side
A circle through B must have its centre at B

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
Statement 1: Exactly one circle passes through any two given points.
Statement 2: The smallest circle through two points A and B has AB as a diameter.
Statement 3: For an acute-angled triangle the circumcentre lies inside the triangle.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Infinitely many circles pass through two given points A and B.
Reason (R): The centres of all circles through A and B lie on the straight line joining A and B.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A right-angled triangular garden has legs 9 m and 12 m. A circular fence through its three corners has radius ___ m.

Match each triangle or situation in Column I with its result in Column II.
Column I: 1. A triangle with angles 35, 55 and 90 degrees; 2. A triangle with angles 30, 40 and 110 degrees; 3. A triangle with angles 50, 60 and 70 degrees; 4. Two points 16 cm apart: the least possible radius of a circle through both.
Column II: a. Circumcentre outside the triangle; b. Circumcentre inside the triangle; c. Circumcentre at the midpoint of a side; d. 8 cm.
True or False: As the centre of a circle through two fixed points A and B is moved away from the midpoint of AB along the perpendicular bisector, the radius of the circle decreases. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The radius is sqrt((AB/2)^2 + d^2), where d is the distance from the midpoint, so it increases as d increases. The smallest radius, AB/2, occurs when the centre is the midpoint.
s: States False
Radius grows with the distance from the midpoint, least at the midpoint (AB/2)

questions.q:
Two points A and B are 12 cm apart.
(a) Where do the centres of all circles through A and B lie? (b) Find the radius of the circle whose centre is on that line at 8 cm from the midpoint of AB.
questions.a: (a) On the perpendicular bisector of AB. (b) Radius = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = 10 cm.
s: (a) Perpendicular bisector of AB

questions.q:
A plot has corners P (0, 0), Q (6, 0) and R (0, 8) on a grid in metres.
(a) Where is the centre of the circle through P, Q and R? (b) Check your answer by finding its distance from each corner.
questions.a: (a) The angle at P is a right angle, so the centre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse QR, which is (3, 4). (b) Its distance from P, Q and R is 5 m each (QR = 10 m).
s: (a) Right angle at P gives centre (3, 4), the midpoint of QR
(b) Distance 5 m from each corner

questions.q: A circle is drawn through the corners of triangle ABC. Rohan turns the triangle about the circle's centre through 40 degrees to get a triangle A'B'C'. Is the same circle also the circumcircle of A'B'C'? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. A turn about the centre keeps every point at the same distance from the centre, so A', B' and C' are still on the circle. Three non-collinear points lie on only one circle, so it is the circumcircle of A'B'C' too.
s: Turning about the centre keeps the corners on the same circle
Three non-collinear points give a unique circle, so it is its circumcircle

questions.q: Neha says the centre of any circle through two points A and B must lie on the line AB. Is she right? Give an example to support your decision.
questions.a: She is wrong. Only the midpoint of AB (the circle with AB as diameter) lies on AB. Other centres lie on the perpendicular bisector, for example a point 8 cm from the midpoint of a 12 cm segment, which is off the line AB.
s: States she is wrong; only the midpoint is on AB
Example: a centre on the perpendicular bisector away from AB

questions.q: Meena claims: 'The circumcentre of every triangle lies inside the triangle, because it is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet.' Is she right?
questions.a: No. The perpendicular bisectors do meet at the circumcentre, but where that point lies depends on the angles. For a right-angled triangle it is at the midpoint of the hypotenuse, on the triangle, and for an obtuse-angled triangle it is outside. It is inside only for an acute-angled triangle.
s: Verdict: no
Right-angled triangle: on the midpoint of the hypotenuse
Obtuse-angled triangle: outside; inside only when acute

questions.q: Show that no circle can pass through three collinear points A, B and C.
questions.a: A centre O would need OA = OB, so O is on the perpendicular bisector of AB, and OB = OC, so O is on the perpendicular bisector of BC. For collinear points both bisectors are perpendicular to the same line, so they are parallel and never meet. No such O exists, so there is no circle.
s: The centre must lie on both perpendicular bisectors
For collinear points the bisectors are parallel
So no common centre and no circle

questions.q: Describe a triangle with side lengths whose circumcentre lies exactly on one of its sides and whose circumradius is 6.5 cm. Justify that it works.
questions.a: Take the triangle with sides 5 cm, 12 cm and 13 cm. Since 5^2 + 12^2 = 169 = 13^2 it is right-angled with hypotenuse 13 cm. The circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, so the circumradius is 13 / 2 = 6.5 cm. Any right triangle with hypotenuse 13 cm works.
s: Gives a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 13 cm (for example 5, 12, 13)
Checks the right angle, 25 + 144 = 169
Circumcentre at the hypotenuse midpoint, radius 6.5 cm

questions.q: Justify that exactly one circle passes through three non-collinear points A, B and C, and say what the circle and its centre are called when A, B and C are the corners of a triangle.
questions.a: Suppose a circle passes through A, B and C with centre O. OA = OB, so O is on the perpendicular bisector of AB. OA = OC, so O is on the perpendicular bisector of AC. As A, B, C are not collinear these two lines are not parallel, so they meet at one point only, which must be O. With centre O and radius OA the circle passes through B and C as well, since OB = OC = OA. The centre is forced to be that single point, so the circle is unique. For a triangle the circle is the circumcircle and O the circumcentre.
s: O lies on the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC
The bisectors are not parallel for non-collinear points, so they meet at exactly one point
Radius OA gives a circle through B and C as well
The centre is forced, so only one circle exists
Names the circumcircle and circumcentre

questions.q:
Four villages P (0, 0), Q (12, 0), R (0, 16) and T (12, 16) are marked on a grid in km. A relief camp must be equally far from P, Q and R.
(a) Show which angle of triangle PQR is a right angle and what that tells you about the camp's site. (b) Find the site and its distance from each of P, Q and R. (c) Is village T also at that distance from the site? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The angle at P is a right angle because the axes are perpendicular, so the circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse QR. (b) QR = sqrt(144 + 256) = 20 km, so the site is (6, 8) and each of P, Q, R is 10 km away. (c) Distance from (6, 8) to T (12, 16) is sqrt(36 + 64) = 10 km, so T is also 10 km away and lies on the same circle.
s: Right angle at P, so the site is the midpoint of hypotenuse QR
QR = 20 km, so the site is (6, 8)
Distances from the site to P, Q and R are 10 km
Distance to T works out as sqrt(36 + 64) = 10 km
Concludes T lies on the same circle

questions.q:
Three villages A, B and C form a right-angled triangle with the right angle at A, AB = 24 km and AC = 7 km. A mobile company can place its tower at A, where it already owns land, or at the point equally far from all three villages, where land costs Rs 2,40,000. A tower's cost is Rs 18,000 for each kilometre of range, and the range must reach the farthest village.
(a) Find BC. (b) Where is the point equally far from all three villages, and how far from each? (c) Find the total cost at each site (range cost plus land). (d) Recommend a site using your totals and give one reason apart from cost.
questions.a: (a) BC = sqrt(576 + 49) = 25 km. (b) At the midpoint of BC, 12.5 km from each village. (c) At that point the range is 12.5 km: 12.5 x 18,000 + 2,40,000 = Rs 4,65,000. At A the farthest village is B at 24 km: 24 x 18,000 = Rs 4,32,000, with no land cost. (d) A is cheaper by Rs 33,000; a reason apart from cost is that the equidistant site gives all three villages the same signal distance, so it could be preferred if equal coverage matters. Either choice with these totals and a stated reason is acceptable.
s: (a) BC = 25 km
(b) Midpoint of BC, 12.5 km from each village
(c) Rs 4,65,000 at the equidistant point and Rs 4,32,000 at A
(d) Reasoned recommendation using the Rs 33,000 difference and a non-cost reason

questions.q:
A potter makes plates on a clay slab that carries two nail marks A and B, 16 cm apart. Each plate's rim must pass through both marks. She fixes a pivot on the slab and swings a string of fixed length around it to draw the rim.
(a) Along which line can the pivot be placed? (b) What is the least string length that can work? (c) Find the string length needed if the pivot is 6 cm from the midpoint of AB, and if it is 15 cm from it. (d) Her string is only 12 cm long. Which of these two pivot positions can she use, and what is the farthest the pivot may be from the midpoint?
questions.a: (a) On the perpendicular bisector of AB. (b) 8 cm, with the pivot at the midpoint (AB is a diameter). (c) 6 cm gives sqrt(64 + 36) = 10 cm and 15 cm gives sqrt(64 + 225) = 17 cm. (d) She can use the 6 cm position (10 cm is within 12 cm) but not the 15 cm one (17 cm is more than 12 cm). The pivot can be at most sqrt(144 - 64) = sqrt(80), about 8.9 cm, from the midpoint.
s: (a) Perpendicular bisector of AB
(b) 8 cm, pivot at the midpoint
(c) 10 cm for the 6 cm position and 17 cm for the 15 cm position
(d) Uses the 6 cm position, rejects the 15 cm one, and finds the limit about 8.9 cm

questions.q: A thread AB pulled tight across a wheel with hub C subtends 54 degrees at the hub. The wheel is then turned through 40 degrees, so the thread lies along a new chord DE of the same wheel. What angle does DE subtend at the hub?
questions.a: 54 degrees

questions.q: A ribbon AB is stretched across a circular clock face of centre C so that its ends are on the rim, and angle CAB measures 35 degrees. What angle does the ribbon subtend at the centre?
questions.a: 110 degrees

questions.q: Two threads AB and DE are stretched across the same wheel and subtend 54 degrees and 48 degrees at the hub. Which conclusion is certain?
questions.a: AB and DE are not equal in length
o: AB and DE are not equal in length
AB and DE are equal because both are chords of one circle
AB is shorter than DE because 54 is more than 48

questions.q: A triangular flower bed ABC has AB = AC, BC = 24 m and the height from A to BC equal to 18 m. All three corners lie on the edge of a circular lawn. What is the radius of the lawn?
In a circle with centre C, M is the midpoint of chord AB and angle CMB is (5x - 40) degrees. What is x?

Consider the following statements.
Statement 1: The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
Statement 2: Two chords of a circle that are equal in length must be parallel.
Statement 3: A chord subtending 54 degrees at the centre is twice as long as a chord subtending 27 degrees.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Chords of a circle that subtend equal angles at the centre are equal.
Reason (R): The triangles formed by the two chords and the centre have two sides equal to radii and equal angles between them, so they are congruent by SAS.
questions.a: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: AB is a chord of a circle with centre O and angle OAB = 28 degrees. Then angle AOB = ___ degrees.
True or False: In a circle of radius 12 cm, the chord that subtends 90 degrees at the centre is exactly half as long as the chord that subtends 180 degrees. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The 180 degree chord is the diameter, 24 cm. The 90 degree chord is the base of a right-angled isosceles triangle with equal sides 12 cm, so it is 12 x sqrt(2), about 16.97 cm, not 12 cm. Chord length is not proportional to the central angle.
s: States False
Compares about 16.97 cm with half of 24 cm (12 cm); length is not proportional to the angle

questions.q:
C is the centre of a circle and CM is perpendicular to chord AB at M. Angle ACM is 38 degrees.
(a) Find angle ACB. (b) Use (a) to find angle CAB.
questions.a: (a) CM bisects the chord, so triangles CMA and CMB are congruent and angle ACB = 2 x 38 = 76 degrees. (b) CA = CB, so angle CAB = (180 - 76) / 2 = 52 degrees.
s: (a) 76 degrees, from the congruent triangles CMA and CMB
(b) 52 degrees from the isosceles triangle CAB

questions.q:
In a circle with centre C, chord AB subtends 80 degrees at C. A chord DE is drawn equal in length to AB.
(a) What angle does DE subtend at C? (b) Using (a), find angle CDE.
questions.a: (a) Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre, so angle DCE = 80 degrees. (b) CD = CE, so angle CDE = (180 - 80) / 2 = 50 degrees.
s: (a) 80 degrees, equal chords subtend equal angles
(b) 50 degrees from the isosceles triangle CDE

questions.q: State the converse of 'Equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre', and name the congruence rule used to prove the statement and the congruence rule used to prove its converse.
questions.a: Converse: chords that subtend equal angles at the centre are equal. The original is proved by SSS (equal radii and equal chords) and the converse by SAS (equal radii with equal included angles).
s: States the converse correctly
SSS for the original and SAS for the converse

questions.q: Sunita says the triangle formed by a chord and the two radii to its ends is always equilateral. Is she right? Give an example.
questions.a: She is wrong. The two radii are equal, so the triangle is isosceles. It is equilateral only when the chord equals the radius, for example when the angle at the centre is 60 degrees; with 80 degrees at the centre the other two angles are 50 degrees each.
s: States she is wrong; the triangle is isosceles
Example: equilateral only for 60 degrees; 80 degrees gives 50, 50, 80

questions.q: Asma claims: 'If CM is perpendicular to chord AB, C being the centre, then triangles CMA and CMB are congruent by RHS.' Is she right?
questions.a: Yes. Angle CMA = angle CMB = 90 degrees, the hypotenuses CA and CB are both radii and so equal, and CM is common to both triangles. These are the conditions for RHS, so the triangles are congruent, and AM = BM follows.
s: Verdict: yes
Right angles at M, hypotenuses CA = CB (radii)
CM is common, so RHS holds and AM = BM

questions.q: On a drawing of a circle with centre C, Rohit measures the angle between chord AB and the line from C to the midpoint M of AB as 78 degrees. Show that his measurement cannot be right.
questions.a: CA = CB, so triangles CMA and CMB are congruent by SAS (AM = BM, CM common, angle A = angle B). So angle CMA = angle CMB, and they add up to 180 degrees on the line AB, so each is 90 degrees. An angle of 78 degrees is therefore impossible.
s: Triangles CMA and CMB are congruent by SAS
The two equal angles at M lie on a line, so each is 90 degrees
78 degrees contradicts this

questions.q: Prove that the perpendicular bisector of a chord AB of a circle with centre O passes through O.
questions.a: OA and OB are radii, so OA = OB. Every point equally far from A and B lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB. So O lies on that bisector.
s: OA = OB because both are radii
Points equidistant from A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector
Hence the bisector passes through O

questions.q: Two parallel chords of lengths 24 cm and 10 cm lie on opposite sides of the centre O of a circle of radius 13 cm. Find the distance between their midpoints and justify each step.
questions.a: The perpendicular from O to a chord bisects it, so the half-chords are 12 cm and 5 cm. The 24 cm chord is sqrt(169 - 144) = 5 cm from O and the 10 cm chord is sqrt(169 - 25) = 12 cm from O. The chords are parallel, so the perpendiculars from O to both lie along one line. The midpoints are on opposite sides of O along that line, so they are 5 + 12 = 17 cm apart.
s: Perpendicular from the centre bisects each chord (half-chords 12 and 5)
Distance 5 cm for the 24 cm chord
Distance 12 cm for the 10 cm chord
Parallel chords give one common perpendicular line through O
Opposite sides, so 5 + 12 = 17 cm

questions.q: In a circle with centre O, chords AB and AC are equal. (a) Prove that O lies on the bisector of angle BAC. (b) If angle BAC = 70 degrees, find angle OAB and explain how you get it.
questions.a: (a) In triangles AOB and AOC, OB = OC (radii), AB = AC (given) and AO is common, so they are congruent by SSS. Hence angle OAB = angle OAC, which says AO bisects angle BAC. (b) Angle OAB = 70 / 2 = 35 degrees, because AO bisects the 70 degree angle.
s: Triangles AOB and AOC with OB = OC, AB = AC and AO common
SSS gives angle OAB = angle OAC, so AO is the bisector
Angle OAB = 35 degrees from half of 70
Explains that the bisector divides angle BAC into two equal parts

questions.q:
A craft kit makes a ring pattern on a wheel of radius 12 cm. A thread AB is stretched across the wheel and subtends 60 degrees at the hub C. Equal threads are then fixed end to end around the rim, each turned about the hub from the previous one.
(a) Find the length of thread AB. (b) The next thread DE is placed so that it also meets the rim at its ends and is equal to AB. What is angle DCE and the length of DE? (c) How many such threads close the ring exactly? (d) Kit A has 5 threads for Rs 60 and an extra thread costs Rs 15. Kit B has 6 threads for Rs 80. Which should be bought for a closed ring, and by how much does it save?
questions.a: (a) CA = CB = 12 cm and angle ACB = 60 degrees, so the other two angles are 60 degrees each, the triangle is equilateral and AB = 12 cm. (b) Equal chords subtend equal angles, so angle DCE = 60 degrees, and DE = 12 cm. (c) 360 / 60 = 6 threads. (d) Kit A plus one extra thread costs Rs 60 + Rs 15 = Rs 75, which is Rs 5 less than Kit B at Rs 80; Kit A with the extra thread is cheaper, though Kit B saves buying twice and either choice with the figures is acceptable.
s: (a) AB = 12 cm, from an equilateral triangle
(b) Angle DCE = 60 degrees and DE = 12 cm
(c) 6 threads
(d) Compares Rs 75 with Rs 80 and decides

questions.q:
A circular lawn has a triangular flower bed ABC with AB = AC, BC = 24 m and the height from A to BC equal to 18 m, with all three corners on the lawn's edge. The tap is at M, the midpoint of BC. The gardener places a fountain O at the centre of the lawn.
(a) On which line from A must O lie? (b) Find the distance MO. (c) Find the radius of the lawn. (d) A fountain with three jets, one aimed at each corner, costs Rs 150 per metre of jet pipe. Plan 1 puts the fountain at O with a feed pipe from the tap M at Rs 450 per metre. Plan 2 puts it at M with no feed pipe. Which option is cheaper, and by how much? Give one reason that could favour the dearer option.
questions.a: (a) On the altitude from A to BC, which is the perpendicular bisector of BC. (b) If MO = x then x^2 + 144 = (18 - x)^2, so x = 5 m. (c) Radius = sqrt(144 + 25) = 13 m. (d) Plan 1: jets 3 x 13 = 39 m, 39 x 150 = Rs 5,850, feed pipe 5 x 450 = Rs 2,250, total Rs 8,100. Plan 2: jets 18 + 12 + 12 = 42 m, 42 x 150 = Rs 6,300. Plan 2 is cheaper by Rs 1,800; Plan 1 puts the fountain at the centre of the lawn, equally far from all three corners, which could favour it.
s: (a) The altitude from A, the perpendicular bisector of BC
(b) MO = 5 m
(c) Radius 13 m
(d) Rs 8,100 against Rs 6,300, a saving of Rs 1,800, with a reason favouring Plan 1

questions.q: A circular pond has radius 26 m. A straight plank 20 m long has both ends on the edge of the pond. How far is the plank from the centre of the pond?
Three straight pipes of lengths 14 cm, 40 cm and 48 cm are fixed across a circular tank of radius 25 cm, each with both ends on the rim. Which pipe is nearest the centre and how far is it?
questions.a: The 48 cm pipe, 7 cm away

questions.q: Two parallel chords of lengths 16 cm and 30 cm lie on the same side of the centre of a circle, 7 cm apart. What is the radius of the circle?
questions.a: 17 cm

questions.q: In a circle of radius 10 cm, chords of 16 cm, 16 cm and 12 cm are drawn. Which statement about them is NOT true?
questions.a: The 12 cm chord is closer to the centre than the 16 cm chords
o: The 12 cm chord is closer to the centre than the 16 cm chords
Each 16 cm chord is 6 cm from the centre
The 12 cm chord is 8 cm from the centre
A diameter is closer to the centre than any of them

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about a chord of a circle.
Statement 1: A chord 4 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm is 3 cm long.
Statement 2: Chords at the same distance from the centre of a circle are equal in length.
Statement 3: If chord AB is farther from the centre than chord DE, then AB is longer than DE.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Two chords of a circle at the same distance from the centre may have different lengths.
Reason (R): A chord at distance d from the centre of a circle of radius r has length 2 sqrt(r^2 - d^2).
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: A chord of a circle of radius 15 cm is 12 cm from the centre. The length of the chord is ___ cm.

Match each circle situation in Column I with its value in Column II.
Column I: 1. Length of a chord 4 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm; 2. Distance from the centre of a 30 cm chord in a circle of radius 17 cm; 3. Radius of a circle in which a 16 cm chord is 6 cm from the centre; 4. Length of the longest chord of a circle of radius 7 cm.
Column II: a. 10 cm; b. 6 cm; c. 14 cm; d. 8 cm.
True or False: In a circle of radius 10 cm, a chord 3 cm from the centre is longer than a chord 7 cm from the centre. Give a reason with the two lengths.
questions.a: True. The longer chord is closer to the centre. The 3 cm chord is 2 x sqrt(100 - 9) = 2 x sqrt(91), about 19.08 cm, and the 7 cm chord is 2 x sqrt(100 - 49) = 2 x sqrt(51), about 14.28 cm.
s: States True
Compares about 19.08 cm with about 14.28 cm (closer chord is longer)

questions.q:
A circle has radius 25 cm.
(a) Find the length of a chord 15 cm from the centre. (b) A chord of 48 cm is drawn in the same circle. By how much is it nearer to the centre than the chord in (a)?
questions.a: (a) Half the chord = sqrt(625 - 225) = 20 cm, so the chord is 40 cm. (b) The 48 cm chord is sqrt(625 - 576) = 7 cm from the centre, which is 15 - 7 = 8 cm nearer.
s: (a) 40 cm
(b) 7 cm from the centre, so 8 cm nearer

questions.q: Chords AB and FG of a circle of radius 15 cm are each 18 cm long. (a) Find the distance of AB from the centre C. (b) State the distance of FG from C without further calculation and give the theorem that justifies it.
questions.a: (a) Half of AB is 9 cm, so the distance is sqrt(225 - 81) = 12 cm. (b) 12 cm, because chords of the same length are at the same distance from the centre.
s: (a) 12 cm
(b) 12 cm, equal chords are equidistant from the centre

questions.q: Explain why a chord at distance d from the centre of a circle of radius r has length 2 sqrt(r^2 - d^2).
questions.a: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, giving a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse r and sides d and half the chord. By the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem half the chord is sqrt(r^2 - d^2), so the chord is 2 sqrt(r^2 - d^2).
s: Perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, giving a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse r
Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem gives half the chord as sqrt(r^2 - d^2), then doubles it

questions.q: Ravi says that a circle of radius 5 cm has a chord whose distance from the centre is 6 cm. Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: He is wrong. The distance of a chord from the centre cannot be more than the radius. As a chord is pushed outward it shrinks to a single point when its distance equals the radius, and 6 cm is beyond that; sqrt(25 - 36) is not a real length.
s: States he is wrong; distance cannot exceed the radius
Reason: the chord shrinks to a point at distance r, and r^2 - d^2 would be negative

questions.q: In a circle of radius 13 cm, the distance of chord AB from the centre is twice the distance of chord CD from the centre, and CD is 5 cm from the centre. Eesha claims CD = 2AB. Is she right?
questions.a: No. CD = 2 x sqrt(169 - 25) = 24 cm. AB is 10 cm from the centre, so AB = 2 x sqrt(169 - 100) = 2 x sqrt(69), about 16.61 cm, and 2AB is about 33.2 cm, not 24 cm. A chord's length is not proportional to its distance from the centre.
s: Verdict: no
CD = 24 cm and AB is about 16.61 cm
2AB is about 33.2 cm, which is not 24 cm

questions.q: Show that in a circle of radius 10 cm there cannot be a chord of length 11 cm that is 9 cm from the centre.
questions.a: If the chord were 9 cm from the centre, its half-length would be sqrt(100 - 81) = sqrt(19), about 4.36 cm, so its length would be about 8.72 cm. A chord of 11 cm would need half-length 5.5 cm and r^2 = 5.5^2 + 9^2 = 111.25, not 100. So no such chord exists.
s: Half-length at distance 9 cm is sqrt(19), about 4.36 cm
So the chord is about 8.72 cm, not 11 cm
Concludes no such chord exists

questions.q: A regular hexagon is inscribed in a circle of radius 10 cm, so that its six corners lie on the circle. Each side is equal to the radius. Find the distance of each side from the centre.
questions.a: Each side is a chord of 10 cm. The distance of a chord from the centre is sqrt(10^2 - 5^2) = sqrt(75), about 8.66 cm, by the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem on the right triangle formed by the radius, half the side and the distance.
s: Each side is a chord of length 10 cm, half-chord 5 cm
Right triangle with hypotenuse 10 cm and leg 5 cm
Distance sqrt(75), about 8.66 cm

questions.q: A point A lies 7 cm from the centre O of a circle of radius 25 cm. Of all the chords through A, find the longest and the shortest, and justify why the shortest is perpendicular to OA.
questions.a: Every chord through A has some distance d from O. The longest chord is the diameter through A (d = 0), of length 50 cm. A chord's length 2 sqrt(625 - d^2) is smallest when d is largest. The perpendicular from O to a chord through A is at most OA = 7 cm, with equality only when the chord is perpendicular to OA. So the shortest chord is perpendicular to OA, at distance 7 cm, with length 2 x sqrt(625 - 49) = 2 x 24 = 48 cm.
s: Longest is the diameter through A, 50 cm
Length 2 sqrt(r^2 - d^2) is smallest when d is largest
The distance d is at most OA, with equality when the chord is perpendicular to OA
So the shortest chord is perpendicular to OA
Its length is 48 cm

questions.q: Chords AB and DE of a circle with centre C have AB > DE, and CF and CG are the perpendiculars from C to AB and DE. Show that CF < CG, and check it for chords of 48 cm and 40 cm in a circle of radius 25 cm.
questions.a: AC and CD are radii, so AC = CD. The perpendicular bisects each chord, giving right triangles CFA and CGD, so AC^2 = CF^2 + AF^2 and CD^2 = CG^2 + GD^2. Hence CF^2 + AF^2 = CG^2 + GD^2. As AB > DE, AF > GD, so AF^2 > GD^2 and therefore CF^2 < CG^2, that is CF < CG. Check: CF = sqrt(625 - 576) = 7 and CG = sqrt(625 - 400) = 15, and 7 < 15.
s: Right triangles CFA and CGD with AC = CD (radii)
Writes AC^2 = CF^2 + AF^2 and CD^2 = CG^2 + GD^2 and equates them
AB > DE gives AF > GD, so AF^2 > GD^2
Concludes CF < CG
Numerical check 7 cm against 15 cm

questions.q:
A circular park has radius 25 m with a fountain at its centre. Three straight paths cut across it, each with both ends on the boundary: paths of 14 m, 40 m and 48 m. Paving costs Rs 600 per metre of path, and a lighting cable laid from the fountain to the midpoint of a path costs Rs 400 per metre. The council has Rs 31,000 for one path.
(a) Find the distance of each path from the fountain. (b) Which path is nearest the fountain, and what does that tell you about its length compared with the others? (c) Find the total cost (paving plus cable) of each path. (d) Which single path should the council build to get the longest walkway within the budget, and by how much does the longest path miss the budget?
questions.a: (a) 24 m, 15 m and 7 m respectively. (b) The 48 m path is nearest at 7 m, so the longer the path, the closer to the fountain. (c) 14 m: 8,400 + 9,600 = Rs 18,000; 40 m: 24,000 + 6,000 = Rs 30,000; 48 m: 28,800 + 2,800 = Rs 31,600. (d) The 40 m path at Rs 30,000 is the longest affordable; the 48 m path is Rs 600 over the Rs 31,000 budget, though it has the lowest cost per metre, so the council could seek Rs 600 more.
s: (a) 24 m, 15 m and 7 m
(b) The 48 m path is nearest; longer chords are closer
(d) Chooses the 40 m path and finds the Rs 600 shortfall of the 48 m path

questions.q:
Meena has a circular rangoli board of radius 17 cm and wants to lay a straight line of beads across it, with both ends on the rim. First she lays a 30 cm line AB. Then she turns a tracing sheet through 50 degrees and finds a second 30 cm line on the board. The board has a central motif that is a circle of radius 6 cm, and a bead line is acceptable only if its distance from the centre is at least 6 cm.
(a) Find the distance of AB from the centre. (b) What is the distance of the second line from the centre, and why? (c) Find the distance of a 32 cm line from the centre. (d) Which of the 30 cm and 32 cm lines clears the motif, and what is the longest line that does?
questions.a: (a) sqrt(289 - 225) = 8 cm. (b) 8 cm, because chords of equal length are at equal distance from the centre (a rotation does not change either). (c) sqrt(289 - 256) = sqrt(33), about 5.74 cm. (d) The 30 cm line clears the motif (8 cm is at least 6 cm); the 32 cm line does not (5.74 cm is less than 6 cm). The longest line that clears it is 2 x sqrt(289 - 36) = 2 x sqrt(253), about 31.8 cm.
s: (a) 8 cm
(b) 8 cm, equal chords are equidistant
(c) About 5.74 cm
(d) 30 cm clears, 32 cm does not, longest about 31.8 cm

questions.q: A spotlight at the centre O of a circular pool sweeps 96 degrees from the rim point A to the rim point B along an arc. A camera on the rim at a point P outside that arc looks at A and B. What angle does it see between A and B?
questions.a: 48 degrees

questions.q: Triangle ABC is inscribed in a circle with centre O and angle BAC = 36 degrees. A rope is pulled from O to B and from O to C. What is angle OBC?
questions.a: 54 degrees

questions.q: AB is a diameter of a circular pond and a lamp post P stands on the edge. The angle PAB measures 28 degrees. What does angle PBA measure?
questions.a: 62 degrees

questions.q: The chord AB of a circle subtends 140 degrees at the centre. A point P on the circle lies on the minor arc AB (the arc with the 140 degree angle at the centre). What does AB subtend at P?
questions.a: 110 degrees

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
Statement 1: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle it subtends at any point on the circle outside the arc.
Statement 2: A diameter subtends an angle of 90 degrees at every point of the circle other than its ends.
Statement 3: If an arc subtends 70 degrees at the centre, it subtends 140 degrees at a point on the circle outside the arc.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees.
Reason (R): An arc subtends at the centre an angle equal to the angle it subtends at any point on the circle outside the arc.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: The major arc AB subtends a reflex angle of 250 degrees at the centre of a circle. A point on the minor arc AB sees A and B at an angle of ___ degrees.

Match each situation in Column I with the angle in Column II.
Column I: 1. The angle at a point of the circle outside an arc that subtends 84 degrees at the centre; 2. The angle a diameter subtends at a point on the circle; 3. The angle at the centre of an arc that subtends 29 degrees at a point on the circle outside the arc; 4. The angle at a point on the minor arc AB when AB subtends 100 degrees at the centre.
Column II: a. 58 degrees; b. 130 degrees; c. 90 degrees; d. 42 degrees.
True or False: An arc AB subtends 60 degrees at the centre of a circle, so it subtends 30 degrees at every point of the circle other than A and B. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. A point on the major arc (outside the minor arc AB) sees 60 / 2 = 30 degrees, but a point on the minor arc sees AB as the major arc, whose reflex angle at the centre is 300 degrees, so the angle there is 150 degrees.
s: States False
Points on the minor arc see 150 degrees, from the reflex angle 300 degrees halved

questions.q:
Triangle ABC is inscribed in a circle with centre O and angle BAC = 52 degrees.
(a) Find angle BOC. (b) Use (a) to find angle OBC.
questions.a: (a) Angle BOC = 2 x 52 = 104 degrees. (b) OB = OC, so angle OBC = (180 - 104) / 2 = 38 degrees.
s: (a) 104 degrees
(b) 38 degrees from the isosceles triangle OBC

questions.q:
AB is a diameter of length 26 cm and P is a point on the circle with AP = 10 cm.
(a) Find angle APB and give the reason. (b) Use (a) to find BP.
questions.a: (a) Angle APB = 90 degrees, because a diameter subtends 90 degrees at any point of the circle. (b) BP = sqrt(26^2 - 10^2) = sqrt(576) = 24 cm.
s: (a) 90 degrees, angle in a semicircle
(b) BP = 24 cm by the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem

questions.q:
In the case where DC extended meets the circle at E outside arc AFB (C is the centre), angle ADC = 50 degrees and angle BDC = 20 degrees.
(a) Find angle ACE and angle BCE. (b) Hence find angle ACB and angle ADB.
questions.a: (a) Angle ACE = 2 x 50 = 100 degrees and angle BCE = 2 x 20 = 40 degrees. (b) Angle ACB = 100 - 40 = 60 degrees and angle ADB = 50 - 20 = 30 degrees.
s: (a) 100 degrees and 40 degrees
(b) 60 degrees and 30 degrees, so ACB is twice ADB

questions.q: Dilip says a diameter subtends 90 degrees only at points of the upper semicircle and not at points of the lower semicircle. Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: He is wrong. The diameter subtends a straight angle of 180 degrees at the centre on either side, so the angle at any point of the circle on that side is 180 / 2 = 90 degrees, whichever semicircle the point is on.
s: States he is wrong; the result holds at any point of the circle
Reason: straight angle at the centre halved gives 90 degrees on either side

questions.q: Ria claims: 'An arc subtends 130 degrees at the centre, so it subtends 65 degrees at every point of the circle.' Is she right?
questions.a: Partly right. A point outside the 130 degree arc (on the remaining part of the circle) sees half of 130, which is 65 degrees, so for those points she is right. A point on the 130 degree arc itself sees the other arc, whose reflex angle is 230 degrees at the centre, giving 115 degrees, so the word 'every' is wrong.
s: Verdict: partly right
65 degrees at points outside the arc
115 degrees at points on the arc itself, so 'every' is wrong

questions.q: A chord AB subtends 38 degrees at a point P on the circle. Tara says a point Q, on the same side of AB and farther from AB than P, will see AB at a smaller angle because it is farther away. Is she right?
questions.a: No. P and Q lie on the circle outside the same arc, and the angle at any such point is half the angle at the centre, so it does not depend on which point is picked. Q also sees AB at 38 degrees.
s: Verdict: no
P and Q are both on the circle outside the same arc
Both see half the central angle, so Q also sees 38 degrees

questions.q: Show that no point on a circle can see a diameter AB at an angle of 80 degrees.
questions.a: A diameter subtends a straight angle of 180 degrees at the centre. By the theorem the angle at any point on the circle outside that arc is half of this, 90 degrees. So every point of the circle sees the diameter at exactly 90 degrees, never 80 degrees.
s: Diameter subtends 180 degrees at the centre
Angle at the circle is half, 90 degrees, for every point
So 80 degrees is impossible

questions.q: AB is a diameter with centre O and C is a point on the circle. Using the isosceles triangles OAC and OBC, show that angle ACB = 90 degrees.
questions.a: Let angle OAC = x. OA = OC, so angle OCA = x. Let angle OBC = y, so angle OCB = y as OB = OC. In triangle ABC, x + y + (x + y) = 180, so x + y = 90. Angle ACB = x + y = 90 degrees.
s: Equal radii give angle OCA = x and angle OCB = y
Angle sum of triangle ABC gives 2(x + y) = 180
Angle ACB = x + y = 90 degrees

questions.q: C is the centre of a circle, D is a point on it, and DC extended meets the circle at E on arc AFB. Prove that angle BCA = 2 angle BDA, and find angle BCA when angle BDA = 33 degrees.
questions.a: In triangle DCB, CB = CD, so angle CBD = angle CDB. Angle BCE is an exterior angle of triangle BCD, so angle BCE = angle CBD + angle CDB = 2 angle BDC. In the same way, triangle ADC has CA = CD, so angle ACE = 2 angle CDA. Adding, angle BCA = angle BCE + angle ECA = 2 (angle BDC + angle CDA) = 2 angle BDA. With angle BDA = 33 degrees, angle BCA = 66 degrees.
s: Triangle DCB isosceles; exterior angle gives angle BCE = 2 angle BDC
Triangle ADC isosceles; exterior angle gives angle ACE = 2 angle CDA
Adds the two results
Concludes angle BCA = 2 angle BDA
Numerical value 66 degrees

questions.q: AB is a diameter of a circle with centre O, and C is a point on the circle with angle CAB = 34 degrees. Find angle ACB, angle ABC and angle BOC, and then check your answer by finding angle OCB from triangle OBC.
questions.a: Angle ACB = 90 degrees (angle in a semicircle). Angle ABC = 180 - 90 - 34 = 56 degrees. Angle BOC = 2 x 34 = 68 degrees, since arc BC subtends twice the angle at the centre that it does at A. In triangle OBC, OB = OC, so angle OCB = (180 - 68) / 2 = 56 degrees, which matches angle ABC = 56 degrees, confirming the answers.
s: Angle ACB = 90 degrees
Angle ABC = 56 degrees
Angle BOC = 68 degrees
Angle OCB = 56 degrees from the isosceles triangle
Compares with angle ABC and states the check agrees

questions.q:
A semicircular open-air stage has its straight edge AB = 26 m, and the curved edge has the circle's centre at the middle of AB. Stage lights at A and B are joined by cables to a performer's spot P on the curved edge. Cable costs Rs 250 per metre. Spot P1 has AP = 10 m. Spot P2 is the midpoint of the curved edge.
(a) Find angle APB at P1 and give the reason. (b) Find BP at P1. (c) Find AP and BP at P2. (d) Compare the total cable cost of the two spots and recommend one, giving one reason apart from cost.
questions.a: (a) 90 degrees, because AB is a diameter. (b) BP = sqrt(676 - 100) = 24 m. (c) At P2, angle APB = 90 degrees and AP = BP, so 2 AP^2 = 676 and AP = BP = 13 sqrt(2), about 18.38 m. (d) P1: (10 + 24) x 250 = Rs 8,500. P2: 2 x 18.38 x 250, about Rs 9,192. P1 is cheaper by about Rs 692, but P2 is the symmetrical centre spot, equally far from both lights, which could favour it; either choice with figures is acceptable.
s: (a) 90 degrees, a diameter subtends a right angle
(b) BP = 24 m
(c) AP = BP of about 18.38 m
(d) Rs 8,500 against about Rs 9,192, with a reasoned recommendation

questions.q:
A circular garden with centre O has gates A, B and C on its boundary, and angle BAC = 42 degrees. A security camera must see both gates B and C in one view. A standard lens covers a viewing angle of 60 degrees and costs Rs 6,000. A wide lens covers 150 degrees and costs Rs 15,000. The camera can be mounted at gate A, or at a point D on the boundary on the arc BC that does not contain A (the nearer side to the chord BC).
(a) Find angle BOC. (b) Find angle OBC. (c) Find the angle at which a camera at D sees B and C. (d) Which mounting point and lens do you recommend, and what does it save compared with the other?
questions.a: (a) Angle BOC = 2 x 42 = 84 degrees. (b) OB = OC, so angle OBC = (180 - 84) / 2 = 48 degrees. (c) D is on the arc BC, so it sees the chord at (360 - 84) / 2 = 138 degrees. (d) At A the angle is 42 degrees, so the standard lens at Rs 6,000 is enough. At D the angle is 138 degrees, which needs the wide lens at Rs 15,000. Gate A saves Rs 9,000; D could be preferred only for a reason other than cost, such as a better view of the road.
s: (a) 84 degrees
(b) 48 degrees
(c) 138 degrees at D
(d) Gate A with the standard lens, saving Rs 9,000, with a stated reason

A parallelogram of sides 6 cm and 8 cm with angles 70 and 110 degrees

Statement 3: If two opposite angles of a quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees, its vertices are concyclic.

questions.q: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral and the side AD is extended beyond D to a point E. If angle ABC = 64 degrees, then angle CDE = ___ degrees.

Match each situation in Column I with its result in Column II.

True or False: In a cyclic quadrilateral PQRS, if angle P equals angle R, then each of them is 90 degrees. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. In a cyclic quadrilateral, the opposite angles P and R add up to 180 degrees. If they are equal, each is 180 / 2 = 90 degrees.
s: States True

questions.q:
In a cyclic quadrilateral PQRS, angle P = (7x - 5) degrees and angle R = (3x + 15) degrees.
(a) Find x, angle P and angle R. (b) The other two angles Q and S are in the ratio 3 : 2. Find them and check that the four angles total 360 degrees.
questions.a: (a) 10x + 10 = 180, so x = 17; P = 114 degrees and R = 66 degrees. (b) Q + S = 180, so the parts are 108 and 72 degrees. Total = 114 + 66 + 108 + 72 = 360 degrees.
s: (a) x = 17, P = 114 degrees, R = 66 degrees
(b) Q = 108 and S = 72 degrees, and the total 360 degrees checks

questions.q:
The segment AB subtends 48 degrees at each of two points C and D that lie on the same side of AB.
(a) What does this tell you about A, B, C and D? (b) If the circle through them has centre O, find angle AOB and give the reason.
questions.a: (a) The four points are concyclic (they lie on one circle). (b) Angle AOB = 2 x 48 = 96 degrees, because the angle at the centre is double the angle at a point of the circle outside the arc.
s: (a) The points are concyclic
(b) 96 degrees, double the angle at the circle

questions.q:
ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral in which AB is a diameter and angle DAB = 70 degrees.
(a) Find angle ADB and angle ABD. (b) Hence find angle BCD.
questions.a: (a) Angle ADB = 90 degrees (angle in a semicircle), so angle ABD = 180 - 90 - 70 = 20 degrees. (b) Angle BCD = 180 - angle DAB = 110 degrees, since the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees.
s: (a) 90 degrees and 20 degrees
(b) 110 degrees from opposite angles adding to 180 degrees

questions.q: Zoya says a quadrilateral whose four angles are all different cannot be cyclic. Is she right? Give an example.
questions.a: She is wrong. A quadrilateral is cyclic when each pair of opposite angles adds to 180 degrees, and the angles need not be equal. For example 80, 95, 100 and 85 degrees: 80 + 100 = 180 and 95 + 85 = 180, and the total is 360 degrees.
s: States she is wrong; only the sums of opposite angles matter
Example 80, 95, 100, 85 with both opposite sums 180

questions.q: Ishaan claims: 'In a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, if AD is extended beyond D to E, the exterior angle CDE equals the interior opposite angle ABC.' Is he right?
questions.a: Yes. Angle CDE and angle ADC form a linear pair, so they add up to 180 degrees. Angle ADC and angle ABC are opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, so they also add up to 180 degrees. Hence angle CDE = angle ABC.
s: Verdict: yes
Linear pair: CDE + ADC = 180 degrees
Opposite angles: ADC + ABC = 180 degrees, so CDE = ABC

questions.q: Hema claims: 'If both pairs of opposite angles of a quadrilateral are equal, the quadrilateral can be inscribed in a circle.' Is she right?
questions.a: No. A parallelogram with angles 70, 110, 70 and 110 degrees has both pairs of opposite angles equal, but 70 + 70 = 140, not 180, so it is not cyclic. Equal opposite angles give a cyclic quadrilateral only when each is 90 degrees, that is, a rectangle.
s: Verdict: no
Counter-example: parallelogram 70, 110, 70, 110 with opposite sum 140
Cyclic only when each opposite angle is 90 degrees, a rectangle

questions.q: Show that a quadrilateral ABCD with angles A = 85, B = 100, C = 90 and D = 85 degrees (in order) cannot be cyclic.
questions.a: The four angles total 360 degrees, so the quadrilateral can exist. For a cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles add up to 180 degrees. But A + C = 85 + 90 = 175 and B + D = 100 + 85 = 185, neither equal to 180. So it cannot be cyclic.
s: States that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees
Computes A + C = 175 and B + D = 185
Concludes it cannot be cyclic

questions.q: A rectangle is inscribed in a circle. Show that the point where its diagonals meet is the centre of the circle.
questions.a: Take rectangle ABCD with angle ABC = 90 degrees. The arc AC not containing B subtends at the centre an angle double 90 degrees, which is 180 degrees, so AC is a straight line through the centre, that is, a diameter. The same holds for BD. Two diameters of a circle meet at its centre, so the intersection of the diagonals is the centre.
s: Angle ABC = 90 degrees is half the angle at the centre, so the arc AC subtends 180 degrees there
So each diagonal is a diameter
Diameters meet at the centre

questions.q: Show that a rectangle is the only parallelogram that can be inscribed in a circle, and say what happens to a rhombus that is not a square.
questions.a: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal. If it is inscribed in a circle it is cyclic, so opposite angles add up to 180 degrees. Equal angles that add up to 180 degrees are 90 degrees each, so every angle is 90 degrees. A parallelogram with right angles is a rectangle, so only a rectangle can be inscribed. A rhombus has equal opposite angles which are 90 degrees only when it is a square, so a rhombus that is not a square cannot be inscribed.
s: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal
Cyclic implies opposite angles add up to 180 degrees
Hence each angle is 90 degrees
A parallelogram with right angles is a rectangle
A rhombus that is not a square has no right angles, so it cannot be inscribed

questions.q: A cyclic quadrilateral ABCD has sides AB = 5, BC = 5, CD = 12 and DA = 12 units. Find its area, justifying each step.
questions.a: In triangles ABD and CBD, AB = CB, AD = CD and BD is common, so they are congruent by SSS and angle A = angle C. The quadrilateral is cyclic, so angle A + angle C = 180 degrees, giving 90 degrees each. Then BD is the hypotenuse of right triangle ABD: BD = sqrt(25 + 144) = 13. Triangle ABD has area (1/2) x 5 x 12 = 30 square units, and triangle CBD has the same area. The quadrilateral's area is 60 square units.
s: Triangles ABD and CBD congruent by SSS, so angle A = angle C
Cyclic, so each of angle A and angle C is 90 degrees
BD = 13 from the right triangle
Each right triangle has area 30 square units
Total area 60 square units

questions.q:
A council must choose a quadrilateral plot ABCD (angles listed in order A, B, C, D) for a park whose circular ring road passes through all four corners. Plot 1 has angles 84, 100, 96 and 80 degrees and costs Rs 12 lakh. Plot 2 has angles 90, 90, 90 and 90 degrees and costs Rs 14 lakh. Plot 3 has angles 80, 95, 95 and 90 degrees and costs Rs 9 lakh.
(a) Check that each plot's angles total 360 degrees. (b) Which plots can have such a ring road, and why? (c) On Plot 1, a lamp stands at E on AD extended beyond D. Find angle CDE. (d) Recommend a plot, saying what the cheapest plot would have saved and why it is unsuitable.
questions.a: (a) Plot 1: 84 + 100 + 96 + 80 = 360; Plot 2: 360; Plot 3: 80 + 95 + 95 + 90 = 360. (b) Plots 1 and 2: in Plot 1, 84 + 96 = 180 and 100 + 80 = 180, and in Plot 2 each opposite pair adds to 180. Plot 3 has 80 + 95 = 175, so its vertices are not concyclic. (c) Angle CDE = angle ABC = 100 degrees. (d) Plot 1 at Rs 12 lakh is Rs 2 lakh cheaper than Plot 2; Plot 3 would have saved Rs 3 lakh over Plot 1 but no circular ring road can pass through all four corners. Plot 2 could be preferred only if the council values a square layout, since it costs Rs 2 lakh more.
s: (a) All three totals are 360 degrees
(b) Plots 1 and 2 are cyclic; Plot 3 is not since opposite angles do not add to 180
(c) Angle CDE = 100 degrees
(d) Plot 1 recommended, with the Rs 2 lakh and Rs 3 lakh comparisons and the Plot 3 reason

questions.q:
Two beacons A and B stand on a shore. A harbour rule says rocks lie inside the circle through A, B and the position of boat P, which sees A and B at an angle of 48 degrees. Boat Q, on the same side of AB, also sees A and B at 48 degrees. Boat R, on the same side, sees them at 55 degrees, and boat S, on the same side, sees them at 43 degrees.
(a) What does the equal angle at P and Q tell you? (b) If O is the centre of that circle, find angle AOB. (c) Which of R and S is inside the circle and which is outside? Explain from the angles. (d) The harbour office wants a one-line rule, using only the angle at the boat between the two beacons, that keeps boats on this side out of the rock zone. State it and justify it using (c).
questions.a: (a) A, B, P, Q are concyclic. (b) Angle AOB = 2 x 48 = 96 degrees. (c) R sees a larger angle (55 degrees), so it is inside the circle; S sees a smaller angle (43 degrees), so it is outside. A point outside sees a smaller angle than a point on the circle, and a point inside sees a larger angle (the exterior-angle argument in the proof of Theorem 10). (d) Keep the angle between the beacons at 48 degrees or less, since a boat seeing 48 degrees or less is on or outside the circle, while a larger angle means it has entered the rock zone.
s: (a) The four points are concyclic
(b) 96 degrees
(c) R inside (55 degrees), S outside (43 degrees), with the reason
(d) Rule: angle of 48 degrees or less, justified by (c)
